bai.moTa: Clocks deeper down run slower; escaping light flashes are redshifted; GPS must account for it
bai.yChinh: The closer you are to a large mass, the more slowly proper time passes compared with far away: $\dd\tau/\dd t = \sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$. Nothing is wrong with the clock: every process there, from atoms to heartbeats, slows down equally. Near Earth’s surface, two heights separated by $h$ differ in clock rate by $gh/c^2$; optical clocks can measure a height difference of just 1 mm, and GPS must compensate for 38.5 microseconds per day. This difference in clock rate is what makes objects fall.
bai.giaiThich:
- A stationary clock at radius $r$ runs at the rate $\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$ relative to a very distant clock, where $r_s = 2GM/c^2$. At the event horizon, this rate approaches 0.
- Nothing is wrong with the clock: less proper time elapses there. Two observers at two heights **agree** that the lower clock runs slower (unlike velocity time dilation in Lesson 6).
- Light flashes emitted at regular intervals below arrive less frequently higher up, and the light is redder: gravitational redshift and gravitational time dilation are one phenomenon.
- Near Earth’s surface, the fractional rate difference between two heights is $gh/c^2$. Measured by Pound and Rebka 1960 (22.5 m), Chou 2010 (33 cm), Skytree 2020 (450 m), and Bothwell 2022 (1 mm).
- GPS: +45.7 microseconds per day from gravity, −7.2 from speed, for a net +38.5.
- A freely falling object follows the path of longest proper time; the height-dependent clock rate bends its world line toward the mass.
bai.conSo.1: **38.5 microseconds per day**: how much faster a GPS satellite clock runs than one on the ground (+45.7 from gravity, −7.2 from speed).
bai.conSo.2: **2.46 × 10⁻¹⁵**: the fractional shift Pound and Rebka measured on a 22.5 m tower in 1960.
bai.conSo.3: **22 milliseconds per year**: how much slower a clock on Earth’s surface runs than a clock very far from Earth.
bai.conSo.4: **1 mm**: in 2022, an optical clock measured the rate difference between two points separated vertically by just one millimeter.
bai.conSo.5: **81%**: the clock rate on the surface of a typical neutron star.
bai.conSo.6: **At the event horizon**, the clock rate relative to far away approaches 0.
bai.hieuDung: **You never feel your own time slow down.** To an astronaut hovering just outside a black hole, a second is still a second. The discrepancy appears only when comparing clocks with someone far away: the astronaut sees the outside universe fast-forwarded, while a distant observer sees the astronaut moving in slow motion. In the film *Interstellar*, 1 hour on Miller’s planet equals 7 years on Earth; so extreme a ratio requires an extremely fast-spinning black hole, whereas our model shows a nonrotating black hole.
bai.nguon: Pound and Rebka 1960; Chou et al. 2010; Takamoto et al. 2020 (Tokyo Skytree); Bothwell et al. 2022 (1 mm difference); Hafele and Keating 1972. Values for GPS, Everest, the Sun, and the neutron star are recalculated from CODATA 2018 and IAU constants; see kiem-tra/kiem-phan-3-cu.mjs.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.1: Use the formula $\dd\tau/\dd t = \sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$ to calculate the rate of a clock near a mass.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Explain why gravitational time dilation and gravitational redshift are a single phenomenon.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Derive and apply the weak-field formula $gh/c^2$ for two clocks at different heights.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Recalculate each contribution to the 38.5 microseconds per day offset in GPS.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.5: Explain why the change in clock rate with height makes objects fall.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.ten: Five stationary clocks around a black hole
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
Five white clocks sit at rest at five depths around a nonrotating black hole. The blue clock in the upper corner is a **very distant clock**, where gravity is negligible. Watch the hands: the closer a clock is to the horizon, the more slowly its hand turns. The number beside each clock gives its rate relative to the distant clock.

$$ \frac{\dd\tau}{\dd t} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{r_s}{r}}, \qquad r_s = \frac{2GM}{c^2} $$

- $\dd\tau$: the time counted by the stationary clock on the spot (its {{thời gian riêng|proper time}}, as in Lesson 6);
- $\dd t$: the time counted by the very distant clock over the same interval;
- $r_s$: the {{bán kính Schwarzschild|Schwarzschild radius}} of mass $M$; $r$: the clock’s radial position.

> [Ví dụ] At $r = 2\,r_s$: $\sqrt{1 - 1/2} = 0{,}707$. A clock there counts 70.7 seconds while the distant clock counts 100 seconds. At $r = 1{,}5\,r_s$: 57.7%. At $r = 1{,}01\,r_s$: under 10%.

> [Lưu ý] Here $r$ is not the ruler distance to the center, but the **circumference** of the circle passing through that point divided by $2\pi$. Lesson 11 explains why the distinction matters. The grid surface is merely a stage on which to place the clocks; its shape represents the spatial geometry, also left to Lesson 11. In this lesson, focus only on the **hands** and **colors**: blue is nearly the distant rate, yellow-orange is noticeably slower, and deep red is almost frozen.

> [Thử ngay] The black sphere inside the throat of the curved surface is the black hole; the glowing orange-red ring is the event horizon. Hover over any clock to read its rate, or click a clock to move the astronaut (gold clock) to that radius.
> [[Close to the horizon|gan]] [[Full view|tong]] [[4× playback|nhanh]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.ten: Nothing is wrong with the clock
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
The large gold clock belongs to an **astronaut** hovering at rest on a platform at $r = 2\,r_s$ (using thrusters firing outward, like someone standing on the floor of the rocket in Lesson 7). That clock runs at 70.7% of the distant clock’s rate.

Nothing is malfunctioning. Every process where the astronaut stands slows down equally: atomic vibrations inside the clock, heartbeats, chemical reactions in cells. That is why the astronaut **notices nothing unusual**: one local second still feels like one second. The difference shows up only when comparing with a clock elsewhere. Put more accurately: **less proper time elapses deeper in the gravitational well**.

Unlike velocity time dilation in Lesson 6, this is not a symmetric case where “each sees the other running slow.” Looking outward, the astronaut sees the universe fast-forwarded; looking inward, a distant observer sees the astronaut in slow motion. **Both agree** on which clock runs slower. If the astronaut flies back out to meet the distant observer, the distant observer will have aged more.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the gold dot at the base of the astronaut’s platform along the curved surface, closer to or farther from the black hole. The gold clock’s hand slows down as you move deeper.
> [[Move astronaut to 8 rs|xa]] [[Move in to 1.2 rs|gan12]] [[Back to 2 rs|ve2]]

> [Lưu ý] Sound: the high tick on the left is the very distant clock; the low tick on the right is the astronaut’s clock. Each tick marks one second on that clock itself (sped up according to the “Playback speed” slider). Near a black hole the difference is large enough for your ears to hear the true ratio without exaggeration: at $2\,r_s$, roughly 7 low ticks sound for every 10 high ticks.

+++ Go deeper: where the clock-rate formula comes from
Outside a nonrotating spherical mass, spacetime is described by the {{metric Schwarzschild|Schwarzschild metric}} (found by Karl Schwarzschild at the end of 1915):

$$ \dd s^2 = -\left(1 - \frac{r_s}{r}\right)c^2\dd t^2 + \frac{\dd r^2}{1 - r_s/r} + r^2\left(\dd\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,\dd\phi^2\right). $$

Very far away ($r \to \infty$) this reduces to the flat spacetime interval of Lesson 6, so $t$ is the time kept by a very distant clock. A clock at rest has $\dd r = \dd\theta = \dd\phi = 0$, and its proper time satisfies $c^2\dd\tau^2 = -\dd s^2$:

$$ c^2\dd\tau^2 = \left(1 - \frac{r_s}{r}\right)c^2\dd t^2 \ \Rightarrow\ \dd\tau = \sqrt{1 - \frac{r_s}{r}}\;\dd t. $$

That is the entire derivation. The factor in front of $c^2\dd t^2$ is less than 1 near a mass: this is the **time part** of spacetime curvature.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.de: Drag the astronaut to the radius where the gold clock runs at **exactly half** the rate of the distant clock (50% rate, within 2%).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.goiY: Solve $\sqrt{1 - r_s/r} = 1/2$: $1 - r_s/r = 1/4$, giving $r = \tfrac43\,r_s \approx 1{,}33\,r_s$. Watch the percentage label beside the gold clock.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
Every 2 seconds on the local clock, the astronaut sends a flash of light outward. The glowing dots climb along the faint track to a **distant receiving station** (the blue dot at the edge of the grid). A card in the control panel records the arrival interval between consecutive flashes.

At $r = 2\,r_s$, the station receives one flash every **2.83 seconds**, equal to $2 / 0{,}707$. It is not that light slows down along the way: every flash travels the exact same path through a spacetime that does not change with time, so each flash takes the exact same coordinate interval $t$ to make the trip. The coordinate time separation between flashes therefore stays constant in transit, and the distant clock measures $2 / \sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$ seconds between arrivals.

A light wave is itself a clock, with each wave crest acting as a “tick.” The station receives wave crests less frequently than they were emitted—lower frequency, longer wavelength—so the light **shifts toward the red**. This is {{dịch chuyển đỏ hấp dẫn|gravitational redshift}}.

$$ 1 + z = \frac{\lambda_{\text{nhận}}}{\lambda_{\text{phát}}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}} $$

At $r = 2\,r_s$: $z = 0{,}414$. Slower time and reddened light are **one phenomenon viewed in two ways**.

> [Lưu ý] The color of each pulse (turning from green toward red as it climbs) only illustrates the direction of the shift, not the actual color of the light.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the astronaut closer to the black hole and listen: the “ping” each time a flash reaches the station grows both farther apart and lower in pitch.
> [[Astronaut at 1.1 rs|r11]] [[At 2 rs|r2]] [[At 5 rs|r5]]

> [Lưu ý] Sound: each flash arriving at the station plays a tone. The astronaut “emits” every tone at the same pitch, 880 Hz on the local clock; at the station the pitch drops by the exact factor $\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$, just like light (down to 622 Hz from $2\,r_s$). The value 880 Hz is simply chosen to be easy to hear.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.de: Drag the astronaut to the position where the receiving station gets flashes **2.5 seconds** apart, corresponding to $z = 0{,}25$ (within 0.05 seconds).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.goiY: You need $1/\sqrt{1 - r_s/r} = 2{,}5/2 = 1{,}25$, meaning an 80% clock rate: $r = 1/(1 - 0{,}64) \approx 2{,}78\,r_s$.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.ten: Near Earth’s surface: the rate difference gh/c²
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
Around Earth, $r_s$ is only about 9 mm while Earth’s radius is 6,371 km, so $r_s/r$ is tiny and the clock rate is very close to 1. Using the approximation $\sqrt{1 - x} \approx 1 - x/2$ gives

$$ \frac{\dd\tau}{\dd t} \approx 1 - \frac{GM}{rc^2}. $$

Compare two clocks, one on the ground and one at a height $h$ above it (small compared with Earth’s radius): the higher clock runs **faster** by the fractional amount

$$ \frac{\Delta\tau}{\tau} \approx \frac{gh}{c^2}, $$

where $g$ is the local gravitational acceleration. This matches the accelerating rocket result from Lesson 8 (a ceiling clock runs faster than a floor clock by $1 + ah/c^2$), with $a$ replaced by $g$. The equivalence principle in Lesson 7 already foretold this.

> [Ví dụ] Raise a clock by 1 m: $gh/c^2 \approx 1{,}09 \times 10^{-16}$, so it gains 9.4 trillionths of a second per day. Earth’s surface compared with very far away runs slower by $7 \times 10^{-10}$, or about 22 milliseconds per year. Live for a year atop Mount Everest and you age about 30 microseconds more than someone at sea level.

> [Thử ngay] The scene switches to Earth. Drag the gold clock up and down the tower and listen: its ticks (on the right) run faster than the base clock’s ticks (on the left), speeding up as you climb.
> [[Ground vs. far away|matdat]] [[Everest|everest]]

> [Lưu ý] The real difference is far too tiny to see or hear directly. Here the tower is drawn about 6,000 times taller relative to Earth, and the rate difference of the tower clock is magnified $4 \times 10^{12}$ times: at 450 m its hand turns about 20% faster than the base clock’s. The numbers printed beside the clock are the true values.

+++ Go deeper: from √(1 − rs/r) to gh/c², line by line
Let $R$ be Earth’s radius. The clock rates at $R$ and at $R + h$ are

$$ n(R) \approx 1 - \frac{GM}{Rc^2}, \qquad n(R+h) \approx 1 - \frac{GM}{(R+h)c^2}. $$

Their difference is

$$ n(R+h) - n(R) \approx \frac{GM}{c^2}\left(\frac1R - \frac1{R+h}\right) = \frac{GM}{c^2}\cdot\frac{h}{R(R+h)} \approx \frac{GM}{R^2}\cdot\frac{h}{c^2} = \frac{gh}{c^2}. $$

The last step uses $g = GM/R^2$ and $h \ll R$. Dividing by the rate itself (nearly equal to 1) gives the fractional difference. Numerically, for $h = 450$ m, the exact formula and this approximation agree to within one part in a thousand.

Another way to view it: $GM/r$ is the depth of the Newtonian gravitational potential $\Phi = -GM/r$. The clock rate is therefore $1 + \Phi/c^2$: **Newton’s gravitational potential is really the fractional slowing of time**, multiplied by $c^2$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Drag the tower clock to the height where it gains **2 nanoseconds per day** over the base clock (within 0.1).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: A day has 86,400 seconds, so you need $gh/c^2 = 2 \times 10^{-9}/86\,400 \approx 2{,}3 \times 10^{-14}$, which corresponds to $h \approx 212$ m.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.ten: Measured: from a 22.5 m tower to 1 mm
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
The fractional shift $gh/c^2$ is so tiny that for decades after Einstein predicted it, nobody could measure it on Earth.

> [Lịch sử] In 1960, Robert Pound and Glen Rebka sent gamma rays from iron-57 along a 22.5 m tower at Harvard University. The shift to be measured was $gh/c^2 \approx 2{,}46 \times 10^{-15}$. Using the Mössbauer effect (recoil-free emission and absorption of gamma rays with an extraordinarily narrow line width), they detected the shift and confirmed Einstein’s prediction to within about 10%.

Today’s optical clocks are precise enough to reveal the effect right on a tabletop:

| Year | Researchers and location | Height difference | $gh/c^2$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1960 | Pound and Rebka, Harvard tower | 22.5 m | $2{,}46 \times 10^{-15}$ |
| 2010 | Chou et al., NIST (USA) | 33 cm | $3{,}6 \times 10^{-17}$ |
| 2020 | Takamoto et al., Tokyo Skytree | 450 m | $4{,}9 \times 10^{-14}$ |
| 2022 | Bothwell et al., JILA (USA) | 1 mm | $1{,}1 \times 10^{-19}$ |

By 2010, raising a clock by 33 cm—roughly one stair step—was enough to see it speed up. In 2022, a team at JILA measured the rate difference between the top and bottom of **a single cloud of atoms** just 1 mm thick.

> [Lịch sử] In 1971, Hafele and Keating flew atomic clocks around Earth on commercial airliners, first eastward and then westward (published in 1972). Their results combined both effects: slowing from speed (Lesson 6) and speeding up from altitude.

> [Thử ngay] Hover over the base clock and the tower clock to inspect the numbers. The “Tokyo Skytree” button moves the clock to the 450 m observation deck where Takamoto’s team placed their upper clock.
> [[Tokyo Skytree|skytree]] [[Ground vs. far away|matdat]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
Each GPS satellite carries atomic clocks and continuously broadcasts its time. Your phone compares the time signals from four or more satellites to compute its distance to each one and pinpoint your location. A timing error of 1 microsecond translates into a position error of nearly 300 m.

A satellite clock drifts relative to clocks on the ground for two opposing reasons:

- **Gravity** (this lesson): the satellite orbits about 20,200 km up, where time runs faster than on the ground by **+45.7 microseconds per day**.
- **Speed** (Lesson 6): the satellite moves at 3.9 km/s, which slows its clock by **−7.2 microseconds per day**.

Combined, the satellite clock runs **38.5 microseconds per day** faster. The GPS system must compensate for this offset in the satellite clocks; without the correction, computed positions would drift by an additional 11.5 km each day.

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “GPS only needs special relativity.” Quite the opposite: by far the larger contribution comes from general relativity, and the two effects have opposite signs. Including only the speed term would even get the sign wrong.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the satellite closer to or farther from Earth. In low orbits, speed wins and the satellite clock runs slower than on the ground. Farther out, gravity wins. The label beside the satellite shows both terms.
> [[Show GPS card|gps]]

> [Lưu ý] The distance from Earth’s center to the satellite is drawn to scale (the dashed circle marks the real GPS orbit), while the satellite and its clock are enlarged for visibility. The hand and ticks of the satellite clock magnify the rate difference by $4 \times 10^{8}$.

+++ Go deeper: recalculating 38.5 microseconds, line by line
Input values: $GM_{\oplus} = 3{,}986 \times 10^{14}$ m³/s², Earth’s radius $R = 6\,371$ km, GPS orbital radius $r = 26\,560$ km, $c^2 = 8{,}988 \times 10^{16}$ m²/s², one day $= 86\,400$ s.

**1. Gravitational part.** The clock rate at radius $r$ is $1 - GM/(rc^2)$. Subtracting the ground rate from the satellite rate gives

$$ \frac{GM}{c^2}\left(\frac1R - \frac1r\right) = 4{,}435 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m} \times \left(1{,}570 \times 10^{-7} - 3{,}765 \times 10^{-8}\right)\ \text{m}^{-1} \approx 5{,}29 \times 10^{-10}. $$

Multiply by 86,400 s: **+45.7 microseconds per day**.

**2. Speed part.** The circular orbital speed is $v = \sqrt{GM/r} \approx 3\,874$ m/s. A moving clock slows by the factor $1/\gamma \approx 1 - v^2/(2c^2)$ (Lesson 6):

$$ \frac{v^2}{2c^2} = \frac{GM}{2rc^2} \approx 8{,}35 \times 10^{-11}. $$

Multiply by 86,400 s: **−7.2 microseconds per day**.

**3. Total:** $45{,}7 - 7{,}2 = 38{,}5$ microseconds per day. Multiplied by $c$, that corresponds to about 11.5 km.

This calculation omits a few small corrections: Earth’s rotation slows a clock at the equator by roughly 0.1 microseconds per day, and slight orbital eccentricity causes small periodic variations around the daily average.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.de: Find the circular orbit where the satellite clock runs **at the same rate** as a ground clock—where the gravitational speedup at altitude cancels the kinematic slowdown from orbital speed (ignoring Earth’s rotation). Succeed within 2 microseconds per day.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.goiY: Set $\frac{GM}{c^2}\left(\frac1R - \frac1r\right) = \frac{GM}{2rc^2}$ and solve for $r$: you get $r = 1{,}5\,R$, or an altitude of about 3,190 km.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.ten: The Sun, neutron stars, and right near the horizon
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
On Earth, gravitational time dilation is less than one part in a billion. On more compact bodies it becomes dramatic. The middle column lists the compactness $r_s/r$ where the clock sits:

| Location | Compactness | Clock rate relative to far away |
|---|---|---|
| Earth’s surface | $1{,}4 \times 10^{-9}$ | slower by 22 milliseconds per year |
| Surface of the Sun | $4{,}2 \times 10^{-6}$ | slower by 67 seconds per year |
| Surface of a neutron star (1.4 solar masses, 12 km radius) | 0.34 | 81%: loses about 11 minutes every hour |
| $r = 1{,}01\,r_s$ around a black hole | 0.99 | 9.95% |
| Event horizon | 1 | approaches 0 |

Light leaving the Sun’s surface is redshifted by 2.1 parts per million. Solar spectral lines are therefore shifted slightly toward the red, by the same amount as a source receding at 636 m/s. Measuring this precisely is challenging because turbulent convection on the Sun’s surface continually shifts the lines back and forth.

Just outside the horizon, the rate approaches 0: seen from afar, an astronaut hovering there appears nearly frozen, with light flashes arriving far apart and deeply redshifted. Yet the astronaut experiences time passing normally.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the astronaut close to the horizon and watch the clock-rate curve in the control panel.
> [[Neutron star surface (2.9 rs)|nt]] [[At 1.01 rs|sat]] [[Show Sun card|mt]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.ten: Why objects fall: rate differences bend world lines
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
In Lesson 6, between two given events in flat spacetime, the **straight** world line is the one with the **longest** proper time; every detour records less proper time (the twin paradox). General relativity keeps this exact rule in curved spacetime:

> [Định nghĩa] A freely falling object follows the world line of **longest proper time** between two events (among nearby paths over a sufficiently short interval). Such a path is called a {{đường trắc địa|geodesic}}.

Now include the fact that time runs faster higher up. Toss a ball upward and catch it 2 seconds later. Which path gives a clock attached to the ball the most elapsed time?

- Going higher **gains time**, because clocks run faster at higher altitude.
- But going higher and still returning on schedule requires moving faster, which **loses time** (velocity time dilation).

The path that strikes the exact balance between gain and loss is **Newton’s parabola**, peaking at 4.9 m. A clock on the ball gains $7{,}1 \times 10^{-16}$ seconds from altitude and loses $3{,}6 \times 10^{-16}$ seconds from speed. Going either higher or lower yields a smaller net proper time.

> [Tóm lại] No force is needed to pull the ball down. Because time runs ever so slightly slower lower down (by about $10^{-16}$ per meter of height), the “straightest” world line curves toward the ground on its own. For slow-moving objects, nearly all of everyday gravity comes from the **time part** of spacetime curvature. Lesson 10 draws this path directly on a curved spacetime surface.

[[Astronaut at 2 rs|r2]] [[Full view|tong]]

+++ Go deeper: maximal proper time yields Newton’s law
For a slow object at height $z$ near Earth’s surface, the clock rate on the object has two small terms: a gain $gz/c^2$ from altitude and a loss $v^2/(2c^2)$ from speed. The proper time from toss to catch is

$$ \tau \approx \int \left(1 + \frac{gz}{c^2} - \frac{v^2}{2c^2}\right)\dd t = T - \frac{1}{c^2}\int\left(\tfrac12 v^2 - gz\right)\dd t. $$

With $T$ fixed, maximizing $\tau$ is equivalent to minimizing $\int(\tfrac12 v^2 - gz)\,\dd t$. The integrand is kinetic energy minus potential energy (per unit mass)—precisely the **action** of Newtonian mechanics! The Euler–Lagrange equation immediately gives

$$ \frac{\dd v}{\dd t} = -g, $$

which is Galileo’s and Newton’s law of falling bodies. Numerically, for $T = 2$ s: $v_0 = 9{,}8$ m/s and peak height 4.9 m; the altitude gain is $\frac{g}{c^2}\int z\,\dd t \approx 7{,}1 \times 10^{-16}$ s, and the speed loss is $\frac{1}{2c^2}\int v^2\,\dd t \approx 3{,}6 \times 10^{-16}$ s. On the true parabola the gain is exactly twice the loss. The lesson’s numerical test suite also checks paths half as high and one-and-a-half times as high: both give less proper time.
+++

bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: The exact same factor as time dilation: two ways of viewing one phenomenon.

bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: An astronaut hovers at rest at $r = 2\,r_s$ around a black hole. How many hours pass for a very distant observer during one hour on the astronaut’s clock?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: The clock rate is $\sqrt{1 - 1/2} = 0{,}707$, so $\Delta t = \Delta\tau / 0{,}707 \approx 1{,}41$ hours. Choosing 0.71 reverses the direction: the distant observer counts **more** elapsed time.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: An astronaut hovering close to a black hole looks down at their own wristwatch. What do they see?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.2: The hands move normally: one second is still one second
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: Every local process slows by the same factor—including the astronaut’s brain and eyes—so nothing locally looks out of place. The difference appears only when comparing against a clock at another location (via light signals or meeting again).
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: Two siblings live on the 1st floor and the 50th floor of the same building for 70 years. Which statement is true?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.1: Each sees the other age more slowly, just as in Lesson 6
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.2: The sibling on the 50th floor ages slightly faster, and both agree on that
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.3: The sibling on the 1st floor ages faster because they are closer to Earth
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.4: Neither ages differently because both remain at rest
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: A higher clock runs faster by the fractional amount $gh/c^2$. Unlike velocity time dilation, there is no symmetry here: signals sent upward are redshifted while signals sent downward are blueshifted, so both siblings conclude that the one higher up ages faster. Over a human lifetime the difference is only a few dozen microseconds (about 36 microseconds over 70 years if the 50th floor is roughly 150 m higher than the 1st floor).
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: A GPS satellite orbits at 3.9 km/s, faster than anything on the ground. Yet its clock runs **faster** than a clock on Earth’s surface. Why?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.1: Because the satellite travels through vacuum
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.2: Because the gravitational speedup at high altitude (+45.7 microseconds per day) outweighs the slowdown from orbital speed (−7.2)
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.3: Because satellite clocks are built to higher precision
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.4: Because velocity time dilation speeds clocks up
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: The two effects act in opposite directions, and the gravitational term wins, leaving a net +38.5 microseconds per day.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: Pound and Rebka measured a fractional shift of $2{,}46 \times 10^{-15}$ on a 22.5 m tower. If the tower were twice as tall (45 m), what would the shift be?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.giai: $gh/c^2$ is proportional to $h$: doubling the height doubles the fractional shift. Picking $9{,}8$ mistakes the dependence for $h^2$.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: Explain in words, without using the word “force,” why a ball released from rest falls to the ground.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: Time runs slightly faster higher up. A free object always follows the world line of longest proper time (a geodesic). Starting from rest, staying at a fixed height does not maximize proper time; instead, the world line of greatest proper time curves downward toward the ground in the exact way that balances the time gained at higher altitude against the time lost by moving faster. Seen from the ground, the ball accelerates downward at $g$. Space around Earth is also slightly curved, but for a slow-moving object that spatial part is negligible (Lesson 11).
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), chapter 6: gravitational redshift, GPS, and the principle of maximal proper time; chapter 9: the Schwarzschild metric.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: R. P. Feynman, *The Feynman Lectures on Physics*, Vol. II, chapter 42 “Curved Space”: the section on clock rates in a gravitational field.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: E. F. Taylor, J. A. Wheeler, and E. Bertschinger, *Exploring Black Holes* (2nd edition): clocks around black holes and GPS, worked out thoroughly with elementary mathematics.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: Pound and Rebka 1960, Phys. Rev. Lett. 4, 337; Chou et al. 2010, Science 329, 1630; Takamoto et al. 2020, Nature Photonics 14, 411; Bothwell et al. 2022, Nature 602, 420.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: A clock closer to a mass (at a lower gravitational potential) records less proper time than a distant clock. Rate: $\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: An atomic clock paced by optical light oscillations (around $10^{15}$ cycles per second); its fractional uncertainty reaches $10^{-18}$, sensitive enough to detect a height difference of a few centimeters.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: A freely falling object follows the world line that maximizes proper time between two events (among nearby paths over a sufficiently short interval).
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: Nuclei bound in a crystal emit and absorb gamma rays without individual recoil, producing an extraordinarily sharp spectral line. Pound and Rebka used it to measure shifts of order $10^{-15}$.
canh.ve-tinh-gps-bay-cao-khoang-20-200:
GPS satellite
Orbits about 20,200 km up. Weaker gravity there makes its clock run 45.7 microseconds per day faster, while its 3.9 km/s orbital speed slows it by 7.2. Overall it runs 38.5 microseconds per day faster than on the ground. Without compensating for this offset, calculated positions would drift by about 11.5 km per day.
canh.thap-tokyo-skytree-nam-2020-takamot:
Tokyo Skytree
In 2020, Takamoto et al. (Hidetoshi Katori’s group at RIKEN and the University of Tokyo) placed two optical clocks at the tower base and on the observation deck about 450 m higher. Their fractional rate difference is gh/c² ≈ 4.9 × 10⁻¹⁴: the upper clock runs faster by about 4.2 nanoseconds per day, matching general relativity.
canh.dinh-everest-song-mot-nam-tren-dinh:
Mount Everest
Live for a year on the 8,849 m summit and you age about 30 microseconds more than someone at sea level.
canh.mat-dat-so-voi-o-rat-xa-dong:
Earth’s surface vs. far away
A clock on the ground runs slower than one very far from Earth by GM/(Rc²) ≈ 7 × 10⁻¹⁰, or about 22 milliseconds per year (excluding the Sun’s field).
canh.be-mat-mat-troi-dong-ho-o-do:
Surface of the Sun
A clock there runs slower than far away by 2.1 parts per million, or 67 seconds per year. Sunlight leaving the surface is shifted slightly toward the red, equivalent to a source receding at 636 m/s.
canh.be-mat-sao-neutron-sao-nang-1-4:
Neutron star surface
With 1.4 solar masses packed into a 12 km radius, the surface lies at about 2.9 rs. A clock there runs at just 81% of the distant rate, losing about 11 minutes every hour.
